text_narrative: Halfway through the afternoon sweep the lower arm of the tower jams at forty-five and will not come down. Ilbert works the crank twice, feels the counterweight chain go loose in the housing, and leaves it. The arm above answers fine. He sends the whole word again with the upper arm alone, letter by letter, and the station down the ridge sends back the sign for a garble and nothing else.
text_nonnarrative: A jammed arm was a fault of the tower and never of the word it spelled. An arm held at forty-five counted as no letter at all, and the letter was read as absent rather than wrong. Slack in the counterweight chain bore on the cause and not on the class. Garble was the class where the upper arm alone sent a whole word, whatever the station on the ridge sent back.

text_narrative: For nine nights running that winter the middle hill of the chain went unwatched, and the keepers at either end of it never owned to knowing. The far end lit on the sixth night for a landing on the coast. The near end lit an hour later off its own reckoning of the smoke. Between them the middle hill stood dark, and the message crossed the county anyway, short by one fire.
text_nonnarrative: Six hills carry the chain along the ridge line, and the middle one is the lowest of them by a hundred feet. Its summit lies in the lee of the two on either side. Sightlines from the far end are clear to the coast and blocked inland. Ground on the near slope is boggy to the top, and the shelter for the watch sits below that, in a fold out of the wind.

text_narrative: There was a horn in the valley that would not sound a fifth, though it sounded every other interval a horn can. The smith who made it had been paid in salt and had counted the sacks twice. Three winters the calls went out short of one note, and the herds came in wrong to the wrong gates, and at the fourth winter a boy blew the fifth by accident and the hill answered it in a voice nobody owned.
text_nonnarrative: Gathering calls stand apart from warning calls in the interval they rest on rather than in their length. A warning rests on a fifth and holds it; a gathering rests on a third and holds no higher. Recall calls are a third kind, marked out from both by their want of any fixed interval at all. Pitch belongs to the horn and not to the class, so two horns a tone apart carry the same three calls.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the line the middle shutter of the sixth frame was found painted over on both faces. The station book for that quarter held no entry against it. Traffic that quarter ran at half the usual count and every word of it was clean. The overseer who came up in the autumn had the paint scraped off, and the count went back to its old figure with the old proportion of garbles in it.
text_nonnarrative: No frame was permitted more than six shutters, and the sixth was to be reserved for the numeral sign alone. Faces were required to be black on the near side and white on the far. Paint on a shutter was allowed only over rust and never over a working face. Where a frame stood within sight of two stations, its middle shutter was to be set for the nearer of them. Entries against a shutter out of use were required.

text_narrative: Nine of the eleven messages on the morning sheet come back repeated word for word, and Verrin cannot make that sit right. A clerk who repeats back perfectly nine times in a morning is a clerk who is copying from the sheet rather than from the wire. She marks the sheet with a cross in the margin and says nothing to the room. The tenth comes back with a fault in it, and she is almost glad.
text_nonnarrative: Repeat-back accuracy varies far more between clerks than between the hours of a shift. The median clerk returns about one message in seven with some fault in the repetition, and the middle half of the values lies between one in five and one in twelve. Clerks with the cleanest returns account for most of the spread rather than the worst, since perfect mornings are commoner in the sample than any run of ordinary ones.

text_narrative: A relay post on the third arm of the northern chain fell out of the circuit for six hours last quarter after its mast alignment slipped nineteen degrees. The two posts either side held the traffic between them at reduced rate. Crews from the coast reset the mast the same night. The interruption was logged as a single break and the messages held during it went out in their original order, none older than a day.
text_nonnarrative: Spacing between relay posts is a function of mast height and of the clarity of the air, and of nothing else in flat country. Where hills stand in the way, the governing quantity is the height of the obstruction rather than the distance. Each post holds a circuit with the two nearest to it and with no others. Without a working alignment at one post the two circuits either side of it are independent.

text_narrative: Before the hills had names the first watchers laid their fires nine leagues apart, and the smoke of them was the first speech the sky was made to carry. One column meant the sea was quiet. Two set a day's walk apart meant it was not. The wind, who had no part in the agreement, learned the spacing in a single season and began to lay false columns of its own along the eastern shore.
text_nonnarrative: Smoke signalling by column count is the coarsest of the visual codes, with a vocabulary fixed at four terms or fewer. Its unit is not the column but the gap between columns, measured in the spacing of the fires rather than in time. Legibility depends on a still air and on a sky pale enough to hold the outline. The code is therefore shallow, and its whole meaning is settled in advance.

text_narrative: Kesta learned the eastern frame in a fortnight and the southern in three days. The night the northern frame was rebuilt with two extra pigeonholes she threw eleven letters wrong in an hour. A month on she could work the new frame blind. The winter they turned the whole rack ninety degrees to the window she was slower than the boy who had started in October, and she stayed slower until spring.
text_nonnarrative: Throw: the placement of one letter into one pigeonhole, counted as a single act whatever its distance. Miss-throw: any throw into a hole adjacent to the right one. Foreign throw: the same fault at a distance of two holes or more, which is a separate class. Blind working: working a frame by the position of the hole alone. Rack turn: a change in the standing of a frame relative to the window.

text_narrative: The outer ring of the wheel turns without a sound, which is wrong, because the detents were cut by hand and every other wheel in the room clicks. Sabel holds it up to the lamp. Twenty-six letters on the inner disc, twenty-seven on the outer, and the twenty-seventh is a character she has never seen in any alphabet. She turns the ring one letter further. The extra character comes round again, in a different place.
text_nonnarrative: A pawl was absent from the smaller wheels, and on those the inner disc and the outer ring were free of each other at every setting. The larger pattern held three parts: a fixed plate, an inner disc lettered on its rim, and an outer ring seated over both. Detents lay under the ring at even spacing. The lettering on the two rims was of equal count on all but the courier pattern.

text_narrative: Nobody on the club's signal crew will hoist under Ferrow now, and it goes back to one race. He has a rule that the substitute flag stands for whatever the crew last sent, and he will not be argued out of it. The rule is right for two hoists in three. On the long numbers it puts a repeated digit one place out, and the whole board reads as a different boat, and that is what happens in the race.
text_nonnarrative: Substitute flags were always the shabbiest part of a hoist code, and the codes that leaned hardest on them were the ones that read worst at distance. What passed for economy in such a system was usually a refusal to buy a second set of numerals. The better codes were the ones that kept the substitute for a single position and never for a run, and even those were poor beside a plain second set of flags.

text_narrative: There was a house that kept its whole account in knotted cord, and a daughter of that house who could read a cord in the dark with one hand. When the cords were taken by a creditor she tied the same accounts again from memory in a single night. The knots came out identical but for one, and that one stood in the place where the creditor's own debt had been, and it counted for twice.
text_nonnarrative: The controversy whether a knotted cord was a record or a message turned on nothing in the cord itself. A record was held to be a thing that stood for a state; a message, a thing that stood for an act of sending. On that account one cord was both, and the two descriptions were not rivals but different ways of counting the same knots. The stronger view was that sending, and not the knot, made the difference.

text_narrative: In the sixth year after the market charter the holding shelf at the gate house was ordered emptied twice a year instead of once. Forty-one packets were burned at the first clearing and nine of them were claimed within the month. Two claimants brought their tallies and were told the tallies now stood for nothing. The clerk of the gate entered all of it under one line and gave the count wrong by three.
text_nonnarrative: A packet is held at the gate house only where no address within the town is given on it, and such a packet is said to lie at call. Where a claimant produces a tally answering to the packet, the holding ends and the packet is deliverable. Nothing in the clearing rule affects a packet under claim. A packet cleared from the shelf is not thereby undeliverable, but it is outside the holding.

text_narrative: Twenty flashes to the minute was the rate on the harbour lamp and Marnie had counted it since she was nine, lying at the top window with the sash up. Tonight it was nineteen. Nineteen was nothing, nineteen was a cold night and a stiff shutter, and she knew that, and she counted it again from the beginning and got nineteen, and lay there working out how long it would take anyone to notice.
text_nonnarrative: Beyond about thirty flashes to the minute a shutter lamp is unreadable at any distance, and below eight the rate is indistinguishable from an unsteady flame. Within those bounds the readable range varies as the inverse square root of the flash rate, and the constant of that relation is a property of the lens rather than of the shutter. The rate under cold is lower by roughly one flash in twenty for every ten degrees.

text_narrative: A station on the outer ring is answering to a call sign issued to a station decommissioned nine years ago, and traffic for both is arriving at the same receiver. The duplicate is not on any current list. Operators along the ring report clean signals in both directions and no loss of messages. The board has withdrawn the sign from service and assigned a third in its place, and the duplicate continues to answer.
text_nonnarrative: A call sign was valid only where it stood against a single station on the current list. Two stations answering to one sign made a position that was void, and neither answer counted. Silence was not an answer and could not be challenged. A sign withdrawn from service was unassignable for five years, and a station holding a withdrawn sign was out of the ring for every purpose but distress and the answering of it.

text_narrative: The three drums of the river people were cut from one tree in the age before the floods, and each was given a voice that reached a different distance. The smallest was heard to the first bend and no further. The middle one was heard to the falls. The great drum was heard by everyone the river had ever carried, living or otherwise, and for that reason it was struck once in a generation and never twice.
text_nonnarrative: Three sizes of river drum were in use, of which the middle was the commonest and the great drum the rarest by far. The small drum was a hand span across the head, hide on one face only, with the shell open below. The middle carried hide on both faces and a cord tension. The great drum stood waist high, was hooped in iron at the waist, and was mounted on a frame rather than carried.

text_narrative: Every capsule Ossian takes off a returning bird holds a message he has already had. The first time it is a note about a delayed cart, arriving four days after the cart. The second time it is the same note in the same hand. By the ninth bird he has stopped opening them and keeps the capsules in a jar, and the jar is heavier each week than the count of capsules in it will account for.
text_nonnarrative: Capsule weight was the wrong constraint to design a pigeon post around, and the codes built to respect it were poorer for the effort. The birds tolerated more than the designers allowed, and the saving in paper bought nothing but a denser hand and a higher garble rate. It was fair to grant that the lightest capsules did fly marginally better in wind. The gain sat well inside the loss in legibility, and the argument stood.

text_narrative: The far mirror answered before the near one had finished its word, which was not possible at that distance, and Peiro kept the sun on it anyway. Nine miles of dry air lay between the two stations. He tilted the mirror off the sighting rod and the answers went on coming, in the same hand, at the same rate. He put the cover over the glass. The last three letters arrived after the cover was down.
text_nonnarrative: Alignment is judged on the sighting rod and never on the answer received. A mirror off the rod is out of alignment whatever letters arrive, and a mirror true to it is in alignment though nothing arrives at all. Distance bears on the cause and not on the class: nine miles of dry air is within the ordinary reach. A cover over the glass puts the station outside the class entirely, since a covered mirror carries no sun.

text_narrative: Everyone on that street could read the chalk on the corner of the tannery wall, which was the trouble with it. A single upright meant a packet was lying under the third step. Two uprights meant the man who left it had been followed. For nine months the marks ran true, and then somebody who was not in the arrangement started chalking two uprights every night for the pleasure of watching the street empty.
text_nonnarrative: Upright: a single vertical stroke, the whole of the affirmative vocabulary. Crossed upright: the same stroke with a bar, meaning the affirmative was withdrawn. Blank wall: the state of a drop with no mark on it, which was distinct from a drop with a stroke rubbed out. Ghost: a mark whose maker was outside the arrangement. Wall hand: the manner of a maker, so far as it was legible in the stroke.

text_narrative: A heron of the marshes agreed to carry the line of a message kite from the low field to the headland, on condition that nothing be tied to it. The kite makers tied a slip of paper the width of a feather. The heron flew the line out to the headland as promised, and set it down, and never came back to the low field, and after that the kites were flown on the wind alone.
text_nonnarrative: Line for a message kite is required to be of hemp and of a single length, spliced nowhere along its run. A tail is permitted only on the smaller patterns. Signalling by line is to be read from the number of tugs and from their spacing, and no meaning is to attach to their strength. Where two kites are flown from one field, their lines are required to stand at least forty paces apart at the ground.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the siege the priority board at the north gate was reduced from five classes to two. Sixty-one messages sat in the middle class on the day of the change and every one of them was entered as ordinary. Four were for the water party. The runner who took them out went by the long lane, which was proper for ordinary traffic, and the water party had moved by the time he reached the ford.
text_nonnarrative: Priority was a property of the message and not of the runner who took it, and a message entered as ordinary was ordinary however it was carried. Classes were set at the board and nowhere else. The water party's traffic ranked by its content, so a class of two admitted no middle case and nothing was graded between them. The lane chosen out of the gate bore on the delay and never on the class of the message.

text_narrative: Two pads left in the tin and both of them numbered eleven, which means somebody at the other end has the same eleven, or nobody has. Sivrit turns them over. Same grain of paper, same ink, same worn corner. Either the printers duplicated a sheet forty years ago or the tin has been opened. He decides it was the printers, because the alternative asks who, and he has been careful not to ask that all winter.
text_nonnarrative: Security in a pad system rested on the pairing of sheets and on nothing in the characters themselves. Each sheet had exactly one counterpart, and the two were held at opposite ends of a single link. The numbering was an index to the pairing and carried no part of the key. Where a sheet existed in three copies rather than two, the pairing was undefined, and the system gave no account of which copy governed.

text_narrative: A listening watch kept at the northern depot last season recorded no traffic across eleven consecutive night shifts, the longest such run in the depot's record. The aerial and the receiver were found sound. The watch was kept by two members of the party in alternation, four hours each. Traffic resumed on the twelfth night at the usual volume, and the eleven blank sheets were entered in the log without comment.
text_nonnarrative: Inside the depot the listening room occupies the north corner, with the receiver bench against the outer wall and the log rack above it. The aerial mast stands forty paces upslope of the building, clear of the ridge to the east but not to the west. Ground between mast and door is gravel and holds no water. The bunk space lies through a single door, so the watch sits within call of the party.

text_narrative: In the years when the sky-writers still had their tower, every message was padded out to a thousand characters with nulls, so that no watcher below could count the length of a thing. The nulls were meaningless by decree. Then one of the sky-writers set the nulls of a whole season in a pattern, and the pattern was read from the ground, and the tower was pulled down by people who had learned to count.
text_nonnarrative: Nulls are called meaningless, and the word does more work than it can bear. A character carries no meaning under the code and yet carries information about the code, and these are two properties, not one. If the second counts as meaning, padding is a species of message and cannot be treated as absent. If it does not, the notion of meaning at work here is narrower than any ordinary use of the term.

text_narrative: Three times that year Delfa was handed a page reference with no book named, and three times she found the book by the shape of the numbers alone. The first was a psalter, from the low line counts. The second was an almanac, from the columns. The third had numbers that fitted nothing on any shelf in the house, and she carried it in her pocket for a month, and then she stopped carrying it.
text_nonnarrative: Running keys were not book codes at all, though the two were often lumped together: a running key drew its material in order, while a book code addressed it by position. Within book codes proper, the page-line-word form was distinguished from the word-count form by what the number indexed rather than by its size. A third form indexed the edition instead of the page, and was useless where two editions stood alike.

text_narrative: Fog on the channel and the whistle from the north bank gives four short and one long, which is not in the book. Aleth waits. The book has one short for a vessel under way, two for a vessel stopped, three for a vessel making sternway. Four is nothing. The whistle gives it again at the same interval, from a little nearer, and there is no vessel on the water between the two banks.
text_nonnarrative: An answering blast is legal only against a blast sounded from another vessel, and a vessel that answers nothing is in a position the code does not define. Four short blasts belong to no legal signal, so nothing answers them and the position stands unresolved. Silence from a vessel under way is a fault and not a signal. Two vessels sounding the same blast at once put both in the wrong, whatever their headings.

text_narrative: Nobody at the way station sets a clock by the down coach any more, and the reason is a driver called Herrick. He runs it early. Not late, early, which nobody expects and nobody can plan against, and the sacks go out before half the town has written. The company has spoken to him twice. He keeps the schedule to the minute on the up run, so there is nothing anyone can put in writing.
text_nonnarrative: A mail coach schedule was a table of latest permitted arrivals rather than of expected ones, which is why early running counted against it as heavily as late. Its intervals were fixed by the slowest stage on the route and not by the mean. Tolerance at each stage was narrow, of the order of a quarter hour, and the tolerance was one-sided. Punctuality was therefore a matter of the table and never of the road.

text_narrative: There was a scribe in the marsh country who could take down a speech faster than it was given, and the guild said it could not be done and sent for the outlines. The outlines were plain enough. Each stood for a word that had not been spoken yet. The guild burned the book and the scribe went on writing, and every speech in that country came out afterwards the way the outlines had it.
text_nonnarrative: Speed is the poorest ground on which to recommend a shorthand, and the systems that chase it are the least worth having. Economy in the tighter outlines amounts to a shifting of labour from the hand to the reader, who must supply half the vowels unaided. The systems worth defending are those legible to a second hand a year on, and these are without exception the slower ones to write and to learn.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the harbour works a lamp of the new pattern was set on the mole head, with four shutters instead of two. The keeper's return for the following winter showed the lower pair jammed on sixty nights and the upper pair on none. The founder was written to and did not reply. In the spring the lower pair was taken out altogether and the lamp worked as the old pattern had.
text_nonnarrative: Four parts make up a shutter lamp of the harbour pattern: the lantern proper, a pair of hinged leaves on either flank, a linkage behind them, and a hand lever at the base. The leaves are hung on pintles set into the frame and not into the glass. The linkage is single on the older lamps and doubled on the newer. A return spring is absent from every pattern with four leaves.

text_narrative: Sixty-two undelivered forms in the drawer and the disposal date is the end of the month, which Nerella has known for a fortnight and has done nothing about. Burning them is the rule. The rule assumes the addressees are gone, and eleven of these are for one house on the quay, and the house is not gone, it is only shut. She closes the drawer. There is a fortnight yet, she thinks, which is what she thought a fortnight ago.
text_nonnarrative: A message was undelivered where no addressee was found at the address borne on it, and undeliverable where no such address existed. The two were distinct and nothing in the disposal rule joined them. Where an address was found shut but standing, the message was undelivered and not undeliverable, whatever the length of the closure. Disposal applied to the undeliverable class alone, and nothing in it affected a message held against a shut house. Disposal date was no part of either class.

text_narrative: A correction sent from the eastern office this week reverses a figure that was never in error, and the original message is now on file in two forms. The office reports the correction as issued against the wrong serial. Both forms carry the same time of receipt. Clerks at the receiving end have entered the later form, as the standing arrangement provides, and the earlier one remains attached to the file unmarked.
text_nonnarrative: Corrections outnumber the garbles they answer to by about three to two across the offices sampled. Most of the excess falls to a small number of offices: five of the twenty-two account for over half of all corrections issued. Within an office the rate is steadier than between offices, and the spread over a year is narrow. Corrections against a wrong serial are rare, at under two percent, and they cluster in the same five.

text_narrative: When the first shaft was sunk the makers hung a bell at the head of it and gave the cage three strokes for down and two for up, and one stroke for a thing that had no name. In nine hundred years the one stroke was rung four times. Each time the cage came up empty and warm. The makers were long gone by the fourth, and the rope was rung by nobody anyone could find.
text_nonnarrative: Audibility of a shaft bell is proportional to the mass of the bell and inversely to the depth, though the second relation weakens below about forty fathoms. The number of distinguishable codes is bounded by the interval a listener can hold, which is of the order of four strokes. Beyond that the count is unreliable, and doubling the rope tension buys nothing, since the limit is in the listener and not in the bell.

text_narrative: Osher franked the first sack of the imperial mail with a die cut two days before the treaty and nobody questioned it. The second sack, in the spring, went out under the same die and came back from the border with every cover refused. He cut a new die in July with the old crown on it and that sack passed. In November the old crown was refused and the treaty die passed, and by then he kept both on the bench.
text_nonnarrative: A cover is refused on the die that struck it and never on the sack it travelled in. The crown borne by a die settles the class; the date the die was cut bears only on the cause of a refusal. A franking struck at the bench after a treaty is of the later class whatever crown it shows. Mail refused at the border is refused cover by cover, and a sack has no standing of its own under the rule.

text_narrative: The serial on the incoming slip read nine hundred and one, and the last one logged had been nine hundred and three. Teoline held the slip under the lamp with the log open beside it. Nothing was missing. Every number between was accounted for, signed, timed. She wrote nine hundred and one at the foot of the page, out of order, and drew a line under it, and the next slip came in reading nine hundred and one as well.
text_nonnarrative: Serial numbers were a poor guarantee of completeness, and the confidence placed in them was largely borrowed from the arithmetic rather than earned by the practice. A gapless run proved only that the numbers were gapless. Duplicates and reissues left no trace in the sequence at all. It was true that a gap was strong evidence of a loss, which was worth something. The converse did not follow, and most of the trust rested on the converse.

text_narrative: Everybody on the terrace knows what the green rocket means and nobody agrees about the red. Half the street holds it is a call for the boat crew. The other half holds it is the all-clear, which is the opposite thing, and both halves have been saying so since before Marda's mother was born. The chandler who sells the rockets will not be drawn. He sells more red than green, every year, and says nothing.
text_nonnarrative: Green, red, white and blue make up the whole of the chandler's stock, and green is the cheapest and the commonest by a wide margin. Green is a single star, burning about four seconds. Red is a single star of the same duration in a heavier case. White is a pair of stars with a half-second gap between them. Blue is the rarest and is sold only in boxes of six, with the case unmarked.

text_narrative: Seven posts stood on that road with a runner at each, and a tally stick split between every two of them so the halves had to meet. A runner at the fourth post lost her half in a river. She cut a new one and matched it to the third post's half, and it matched, and matched the fifth as well, and the road ran on for years on a stick that had never been split at all.
text_nonnarrative: A tally was in force between two posts only while both halves were in the hands of the runners of those posts, and not otherwise. Where a half was lost, the tally was void as between those two posts and unaffected as between any other pair. A half cut to replace a lost one was a new half and no part of the old tally. Nothing in the rule of replacement gave the new half the standing of the old.

text_narrative: In the third season of the packet run the speaking tubes were relabelled forward to aft instead of by deck, and the change was entered in the ship's book on a single line. For eleven days the calls went to the wrong stations. The mate who had ordered it kept a count and made the count seventy-four. On the twelfth day the old plates were screwed back over the new ones and the count stopped at seventy-four.
text_nonnarrative: Labelling a tube network by position rather than by function looks like the more durable scheme and is in fact the more fragile one. Positions hold only while the fittings do; functions survive a refit. The usual defence is that position needs no learning, and this is true of a newcomer on the first day. It is false of everyone else aboard, and the scheme is paid for daily by the many to spare the few.

text_narrative: Eleven strokes on the muster gong and the yard was full before the eleventh had finished, which was the part Ilva could not get past. Eleven meant assemble. Eleven had always meant assemble. But the yard had been empty at the first stroke and full at the tenth, and nobody had come through the gate, and she had been watching the gate the whole time because watching the gate was the whole of her work.
text_nonnarrative: A muster was counted from the gong and never from the yard. Eleven strokes stood for assemble whatever number of them was heard, so a count broken at the tenth was still eleven and still assemble. Presence in the yard bore on the return and not on the class of the call. The gate was no part of the criterion, and a watch kept at the gate the whole time settled nothing about who was mustered.

text_narrative: The counting office has ruled that a hyphenated compound stands as one word for charge, reversing a practice of nineteen years, and the ruling applies to traffic already lodged. Six hundred and forty messages lodged this week fall under it. The office states that no refund arises, since the earlier count was correct under the earlier rule. Clerks at four branches are entering both counts on the docket, which the ruling neither requires nor forbids.
text_nonnarrative: Every group of characters bounded by spaces was to be charged as one word, and a group of more than fifteen characters was to be charged as two. Figures were permitted in a group with letters only in an address. The signature was required to be charged and the address was not. Where a sender lodged a message with the count entered, the office was to accept that count unless it stood short by three or more.

text_narrative: In the age when the world was still plumbed with the old pipes, the makers left a tapping code in them so the deep places could answer the high ones. Three taps asked. Two answered. One was a refusal and could not be argued with. The pipes outlasted the makers by a great while, and the taps went on, and by the end nobody knew which end of the world was asking and which was refusing.
text_nonnarrative: Three taps constituted a question, and a question left standing for the space of a hundred beats lapsed and could not be revived. Two taps were an answer and were legal only where a question stood open. A single tap was a refusal, which was not an answer and could not itself be answered. A run of taps beyond three was no signal at all, and the line was held to be silent while it lasted.

text_narrative: The receipt book goes back to Tavi four times in one month with the same mark in it, a small circle. Nobody at that address will own to making it. The first time she takes it for a thumbprint. The second time she takes it for a coin rubbing. By the fourth she has stopped taking it for anything and just carries the book back and rules a line under the page.
text_nonnarrative: Hand receipt: a signature taken at the door from the addressee in person. Household receipt: the same, taken from anyone resident at the address, which was a lesser class. Mark: any sign other than a signature, valid where the maker was known to the carrier. Blind mark: a mark whose maker was unknown, which stood as no receipt. Refusal: the state of a delivery where no receipt of any class was obtainable.
